review: I'm and old grandpa nearing 70 who as played Minecraft with grandkids for about five years. I've been playing Scrap Mechanic for about a week. I highly recommend it. Color, sound, and realism is just right. It's a little like a great day at Disneyland. The in-game help and video tutorials are adequate for a beginner like me. The game play is well designed. It is a creative challenge. I hope the devs write better docs on the APIs and modding. I would like to be able to grow trees and to plant crops anywhere -- rooftops and rocky mountain tops, and not just dirt surfaces.

I have a life, I do not care how much time development took, they delivered on what they promised.
This game was a great value since day 0 of the early access, it definitely is now.

Personally I love any game that gives the player the ability to create and build things. And if you're like me then this game will not dissapoint. As I'm writing this review the game is still in early development but still has lots of interesting 'mechanics' that allows the player to run wild with their imagination! Very excited for the future updates, I hope the devs continue to add new items/mechanics. 10/10 would Scrap Mechanic again. - Squiddy

TLDR:

I love Scrap Mechanic. I mean that sincerely. There is something genuinely special about a game that gives you a pile of junk and basically says, “figure it out.” I’ve spent an absurd amount of time building things that absolutely should work, and then laughing while they spectacularly fail. When Scrap Mechanic works, it creates moments of genuine ingenuity that feel magical.

And yet, despite how much I love it, I cannot honestly recommend it to most people.

The problem isn't that the game is difficult, grindy, janky, or very ... very frustrating. It is, and those things can be part of its charm. The problem is that Scrap Mechanic repeatedly makes understanding its problems part of the skill requirement while doing remarkably little to help players develop that understanding. Its physics make building harder than it needs to be, its progression makes mistakes disproportionately expensive, the Seeker Bot adds frustration without enough payoff, and its quests largely miss an opportunity to teach players how to actually become a Scrap Mechanic.

After 45 years of development, it feels like a game designed for engineers who got bored with real physics and wanted to wrestle with cartoon physics instead.

THE REVIEW:

This is a game about building contraptions for resource collection, mining, transportation, farming, and defense. You have bearings, engines, suspension, weight distribution, logic gates, sensors, controllers, and countless other systems to learn. Then, on top of all that, you have to learn how the physics engine itself misbehaves when you combine them.

Most of my friends who played eventually left because they couldn't make a vehicle behave. Their car flips, slides uphill, or bounces while parked on flat ground. To someone who understands the physics, these are funny engineering puzzles. To everyone else, it feels like the game is refusing to cooperate, like the physics are broken.

When 1.0 added vehicle-related building quests, I thought this might finally bridge that gap. Instead, they were essentially visually different versions of the tutorial car. That was a huge missed opportunity.

The game could have given players a competent explorer, driller, and hauler, each demonstrating different mechanical concepts. Lorenzo could even have found an old mining vehicle blueprint in a trash pile, with an emphasis on sticky wheel / suspension interaction. Nothing spectacular, just understandable and spark creativity.

Beginners could simply use the machines to progress. Intermediate players could take them apart and learn from them. Veterans could ignore it, or just built it for the unlockables. Instead, the builder quests often feel like game playtime padding. They mostly serve as cute diversions without adding much to the game itself.

The community has had to fill that gap. There are countless tutorials explaining Scrap Mechanic's mechanics and countless Steam Workshop creations that function as examples and teaching tools. That's wonderful, but the sheer prevalence of them is also evidence of the problem. Players clearly need instruction the game isn't providing.

The Workshop could have been the perfect answer: download a functioning machine, use it, take it apart, modify it, and learn from it. The problem is that many of the players who need that help never make it that far. By the time the Workshop becomes a useful survival resource (in Scrap City Garage), they've already quit.

The community has built the scaffolding, but the game puts the scaffolding on the other side of the wall.

The component kit grind compounds this problem enormously.

I don't mind grinding in games. Resource gathering fits Scrap Mechanic. The problem is when grinding becomes the price of making a mistake. Other than affecting players who want to build enormous monstrosities it disproportionately affects players who simply don't know what they're doing yet.

There is something uniquely demoralizing about spending 60 component kits upgrading four suspensions, only to discover that the suspension wasn't actually the issue. You've effectively been charged for being wrong.

For a beginner, that's dangerous territory. You're asking a frustrated player to spend another three or more hours grinding before they can afford another attempt at the problem they were already struggling with. That's rage-quit territory. It's not simply, “This game has a grind.” It's, “This game has made experimentation expensive.”

It gets worse in the late game. Once a wall and spudling gun aren't enough to defend your farm, a full blueberry farm require multiple heavily upgraded components costing hundreds of kits. You're potentially looking at 10+ hours of grinding just to reach the next difficulty level, only to risk losing those upgrades in a raid.

For an experienced player, perhaps that's part of the challenge. For everyone else, it's a tremendous punishment for engaging with one of the game's core systems.

Then there is the Seeker Bot.

I suspect it affects different players differently because I'm not particularly bothered by it. And yet even I have had moments where I think, what is fecking the point of this thing?

An invincible, rocket-launching, roaming no-go zone is strange choice. It feels like Scrap Mechanic violates a major design principle: don't put something in your game that the player is not supposed to play with. There are games that use this idea extremely well. Subnautica's Ghost Leviathans patrol the Void outside the playable world, clearly establish a boundary, create tension, and reinforce the idea that there are places you simply aren't meant to go. More importantly, you understand exactly why they're there.

I don't get that same feeling from the Seeker Bot. Maybe it's for tension, or lore, or keeping players away from roads. Even so, I don't think the Seeker Bot is a particularly good solution to any of those. Even if you're not bothered it can still be frustrating.

I've had the thought: “Okay, I'm going to head back to base, unload my junk, get my materials processing, feed my Glowbies, maybe build a roof, and then go to bed.” *sees Seeker Bot in my way* “...Fine game. I'll just go to bed.”

That's friction.

And that's the larger problem with Scrap Mechanic: too much of its difficulty comes from friction instead of challenge. A good engineering challenge asks you to understand a system and use that knowledge creatively. Scrap Mechanic asks you to understand the systems, understand the 10 physics jank options, grind the resources, avoid an invincible missile robot, and then hope your machine doesn't misbehave.

When all of that works, Scrap Mechanic is incredible. When it doesn't, it feels like fighting the game not playing it.

I can't help wondering whether the game needed to be in the hands of players much more aggressively throughout the entire development period (or at all). Not simply playtesting, but continual exposure to people who weren't already good at the game. Because I think it's the missing perspective. Someone who already understands the jank can't understand the lack of intuition new players have for it. 

The irony is that Scrap Mechanic already has what it needs to teach players. It just doesn't provide enough examples. give a machine that works that I can take apart. Let me see why it works, modify it, break it. Give me a faulty farm defense to fix quest. That would turn the game's jank from a wall into a language.

I don't want Scrap Mechanic to become a perfectly polished engineering simulator. The absurd physics, ridiculous machines, and spectacular failures are part of what makes it special. I just want that weirdness to be accessible.

And that's why I can't recommend it without a huge asterisk. If you're down to spend dozens of hours grinding and troubleshooting why a simple design fails half the time, you may love this game. If not there's a good chance you'll quit long before you discover what makes Scrap Mechanic great.

I don't write many game reviews, but I felt it was necessary to write one for Scrap Mechanic. So here's the basic rundown of the game in my mind and in this review I will be listing items that I think should be addressed.

[h1] My Experience So Far [/h1]
So far on this game at the time of writing this review I have almost 16.5 hours played. As far as Early Access games go, this one is by far the most advanced from Launch Date that i've ever
seen on Steam, from Launch it had more than enough to keep you busy for hours on end right out of the gates, not very many games can say that. I started off watching the Videos on the game's 
page like the Introducing ones that showcased the Controller, Thruster etc etc, then as I experimented and numerous trial and error situations, I started getting better and better at knowing
what was going on and how things click. I started with a little piddly concrete car with a horendous design, but then I started to get more intricate with my designs, using pipes and I-Beams
to make an overall badass design, then I found out the steering mechanics and how to work the controller with ease, once all this clicked I made some of my best creations.

[h1] Multiplayer [/h1]
As fun as this game is when you're alone, I thought to myself, "Wow, this would be so fun if I had some buds to play this game with." Sure enough this game was already equipped with a 
Multiplayer from Launch! At first that seems amazing, but then once you start getting a total of 4 players and even sometimes 2 players, the servers lag tremendously, my friends and I 
both checked and we came to the conclusion that it was in fact server side lag, now I know the game came out almost a week ago, but I think that Dedicated Servers should be a rather large
priority for a game of this proportion. Overall, the Multiplayer in this game is rather flawless when I doesn't lag, it makes for an amazing experience with friends and it has so much potential
like the rest of this game. My rating for the Multiplayer alone is a solid:

8/10- This rating due to the Server Side Lag, which can be fixed in the future, otherwise, its spotless.

[h1]This review is for the current version of the game(2/1/16)[/h1]

[b]What is Scrap Mechanic?[/b] Scrap Mechanic is a 3d sandbox where you can construct all kinds of things. From spider mechs to transforming houses, the things you can make are surprisingly vast considering how early in development this game is. The best part? They are planning to add plenty more, which will open up your options to even greater extents.

[b]Positives[/b]:
[list]
[*]This game has a pleasing aesthetic...............
[*]There's no limit to how complex/big your creation can be.
[*]You can set up your vehicle to have multiple passengers, or "co-pilots"(Useful for aircrafts and mechs).
[*]You can automate things. (Spinning windmill, elevators, etc)
[*]The game actually has pretty good physics for the most part.
[*]Decent variety of materials to use.
[*]Quick load times.
[*]Drop in/drop out multiplayer works flawlessly.
[*]You can make games within this game! Like what me and my friend did [url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qdjgM58s4K0]in this video[/url].
[*]This game doesn't take a lot to run, has pretty low minimum requirements for a 2016 game.
[*]A survival mode is planned for the game.
[*]Devs seem to be fairly active on the forums
[*]There's 2 maps, one with terrain and one flat-world for those who just want to build.
[*]You can create, (auto)save, and load back into multiple worlds.
[*]There are in-game tutorials to help you out; they are well designed and easy to understand.
[/list]

[b]Negatives[/b]:
[list]
[*]The game can lag pretty bad, even on high end PC's(especially in multiplayer)
[*]The maps are kinda small, but plenty big enough to have fun in.
[*][strike]The game will crash from time to time.[/strike] Fixed for the most part.
[*]Sometimes you'll run into weird bugs while building more complicated things.
[*]Intense rubberbanding can occur after long playtimes on multiplayer
[*]When in a semi-fast vehicle, your character twists and warps backwards because it can't keep up with the speed.
[*]The triggers (buttons, sensors, switches) only work one way. (i.e. You can't hook up two switches to a single door for inside/outside)
[*]Other people can build on/destroy your stuff
[*][strike]Devs don't seem to have a roadmap[/strike] Devblogs are being released with this info.
[*]At this time, there's no real "point" to making things. Those looking for "objectives" will want to wait.
[/list]

[b]So is it worth it?[/b]
Absolutely. This game is extremely fun for what it currently is. You'll find yourself figuring out how to make your vehicle faster, or how to climb hills better, to not flip over, and so on. Before you know it, you'll have spent 3 hours improving it to perfection. Then you'll find yourself thinking of new ideas you'll want to try, even while not playing the game. I can easily recommend this game to anyone who enjoys creative sandboxes like Minecraft or Garry's Mod. Although this game has a fair amount of negatives, they do not make the game unplayable by any means, and they certainly don't outweigh the positives. If you can, you should pick this game up for sure.

[h1]Stuck in Early Access Hell – Don't Waste Your Time or Money[/h1]

I've been keeping an eye on Scrap Mechanic for what feels like forever, ever since it hit early access back in 2016. At first, it was this super cool creative sandbox with endless building potential, and I was all in, hoping it'd evolve into something amazing. But here we are, almost 10 years later, and it's still "early access"? Come on, that's just ridiculous. It's like the devs are content to let it sit there gathering dust while we wait for miracles that never come.

The "latest" updates? Yeah, those ones from October and December 2024 were basically just bug fixes and tiny tweaks – nothing that moves the needle. Smoothed out some physics glitches and added a few bits, but where's the real content? The last actual major update was way back on May 7, 2020, when they dropped Survival Mode. That was awesome at the time – added enemies, crafting, a whole world to explore – but that was FIVE YEARS AGO! Since then, it's been radio silence on anything big. Sure, there's been some activity on the test branch a few months back, but why the hell has it taken nearly a decade to get... well, not much further? The game's got so much potential with its building mechanics, but it's wasted if no one's pushing it forward.

The community is pissed, and I get it. Steam forums and reviews are full of people calling it abandoned, complaining about zero communication from Axolot Games. No roadmaps, no timelines, just vague promises. It reminds me of Star Citizen – another perma-EA nightmare where you sink time and money into a black hole. If you're thinking of buying this, do it only if you've got friends to build crazy contraptions with; solo, it's just frustrating if you don't know what you're doing. Otherwise, wait for someone else to come along and do the concept better, because this one's treading water.

5/10 – Great idea, poor execution and even poorer support. Unless they wake up and start delivering, skip it. (My review encompasses the company along with the game)

Edit (8/12/2025): Just popping back to say, don't give these devs your cash yet, wait for them to leave early access then you can buy, because this is one of those games that'll never see the end of EA, and if you do want to get your hands on it, wait for a sale because it's definitely not worth full price for promises.

Scrap Mechanics allow me to create cars, houses, and engineering things like elevators, escalators, etc.

- You can't move specific parts without having to delete it and then make another one in different spot (ex: Move engine from the back to the front or more the button up a bit)

- Add a wireless remote control

A Fun, Yet Ultimately Disappointing Experience

After spending considerable time in the world of 'Scrap Mechanic', a game that's been on the market for seven years, I find myself at a crossroads in terms of my recommendation. This title, at its core, is undeniably fun, especially when playing with friends. The collaborative elements and creative freedom offer an engaging experience that shines in multiplayer mode. However, this enjoyment is marred by significant drawbacks that cannot be overlooked.

One major issue is the story mode. Initially, it presents an intriguing concept filled with potential, but this quickly dissipates as you encounter its limitations. The deeper you delve into the structures and the world, the more apparent the game's unfinished nature becomes. Game breaking bugs are not just occasional annoyances; they are frequent enough to halt progress and diminish the overall experience.

Despite being in the market for several years, 'Scrap Mechanic' still feels like it's stuck in an early alpha stage. The lack of development progress is disheartening. It's as if the game has been abandoned by its developers, leaving a skeleton of what could have been a fully fleshed-out adventure. This sentiment is further exacerbated by the developers' habit of promising new content and updates, which, as time has shown, seem to be empty promises. This "carrot on the stick" approach does little more than build false hope among the player base.

It's a peculiar situation. On one hand, I thoroughly enjoyed the initial stages of the story mode and was genuinely excited about the potential 'Scrap Mechanic' had. There were moments of true enjoyment and creativity. However, after years of waiting for improvements and content that never materialized, my patience and enthusiasm have waned.

In conclusion, while 'Scrap Mechanic' can offer fun moments, especially in multiplayer, the myriad of issues, from game breaking bugs to unfulfilled developer promises, overshadow these positives. It's with a heavy heart that I find myself unable to recommend 'Scrap Mechanic'. The game, in its current state, is a shadow of what it could have been, and it's a disappointment to see such potential go to waste.

There's a great deal to already like about Scrap Mechanic, with more on the horizon as development continues.

Scrap Mechanic has the feel of 'Raft' (comforting easy graphics - you don't need a 6 month or younger PC to run it) combined with the block accessorizing of Minecraft (and then some), with a sprinkling of Engineering know-how being handy, and a small helping of Farmville (the engaging side of it).  One of the most entertaining 'building' games I've played in quite a while.  There is a great community, with a number of Video posters providing content (and great ideas!) along with a very active community workshop in Steam for any sort of creation you can dream up.

Likes / Pros
The capability to create/build functional suspension and gearing on vehicles (not needed but awesome!)
Recordable physical actions (creations can change shape, come to life, open/close, raise/lower, drive/fly/float/dive, etc)
Multi-Player friendly - get your best pals together for a session!
Survival/Creative Mode are a blast - I do think Challenge needs revamping - take some ideas from all the content creators!
Good sized world to explore - items created are static, world items taken will respawn after a game day it seems and 'dropped' items despawn after time, allowing for clutter-free world.

Wishes
Static server capability (User created and maintained, but static for better multi-player involvement)
Better water physics - At least some resistance so paddle boats and the like would work.  Something tells me 'liquids' are on the list to get tweeked still, given the liquids used in game and how they can be moved around - and all the pipe pieces in game with no current function.
Ability to import/export blueprints in Survival. (Lots of ability for 'abuse' here, but it still would be nice to reload my 'own' Survival creations for easier creation, if I have the materials on hand to build)
More variety to the bots, with more specific bot AI for the various types (work in progress - bots just got a recent AI update)

Cons
Physics at times can drain FPS rate if 'thing go wrong'  (When they do, it's a panic to find 'what' broke and remove/fix it).  Not only things you create, but in the world if you leave things in disarray (lag can occur in specific areas/tiles if you left that area/tile in a state of ruin - say a wood building knocked over, with bits all sliding around not coming to rest).  This also gets better with updates.  (I feel like SM's creators should talk to Astroneer's creators - lots to gain both ways I think.)

Can't wait for more storyline, perhaps more 'quest' goals in Survival, etc.

If you like building your own unique, functional creations be they buildings, vehicles, or just artwork in the game world you are playing 'in' - then you should pick this up for sure.

Scrap Mechanic или скрап механик  кто как хочет так и называет. Обычные люди подумают лишь о простой песочинице, в которой ты можешь построить простую машинку и не боле. А для истинных механиков это смысл жизни во плоти, не каждый сможет это почувствовать или ощутить. Этот благой дар приходит с сотнями и тысячами часами, лишь единицы смогут осилить и просидеть взаперти в этой визуальной клетке, не каждый сможет освоить принципы этой вселенной. За простыми силуэтами роботов и построек кроется жестокая картина, смотря на которую ты не сможешь оторваться от нее, и покинуть этот мир. Ты будешь сидеть сутками смотря в экран, и не понимать что же тебя держит, даже тянет внутрь этого света. Все в этом мире за тебя решила не судьба, а скрап механик. Все твои действия все твои решения ведут тебя обратно в эту жестокую, ненавистную программу для промывки мозгов. Аксолотли - это группировка по пленению своих пользователей в их визуальную клетку для пыток. Они сделают все чтобы ты зашел туда и начал строить. Они высосут из тебя всю жизненную энергию оставят тебя бес сил и рассудка. Ты будешь зомбирован и одновременно ненавидеть и любить это место. Внутри твоего разума остается твое "я" и ты боришься с их гипнозом, но это не может продолжаться вечно, в конечном итоге твоя душа отвернется от тебя и поведет за собой в скрап механик. Все подчиненные этого проекта ведут себя одинаково. Они заходят в плен и строят по указаниям аксолотлей. Бывали случаи, когда Аксолотль не уследил за проворным механиком, и тот начинал догадывапться обо всем. В такие моменты клетка открывалась и механик был свободен на время. Но после таких выходок скрап механик решал повернутся спиной к механику и навести на него всю не удачу. В прошлых моментах когда твой проект работал и функционировал как решал ты, теперь будет работать как решил скрап механик. Мне самому сложно описать все эти чувства, но мне кажется, что скрап механик добрался до моей головы и принимает некоторые решения за меня. Я заметил, что в моей повседневной жизни стали чаще появлятся моменты не осознованного распространения информации об игре. Это были проявления скрап механика в моем разуме. Он добрался до меня и пользуется мной как распространителем этой жестокой ловушки. Я ничего не могу поделать, процесс запущен, и его не остановить. Besides how beautiful the game is and how satisfying a lot of its mechanics are, what surprises me most is how robust the AI is. After playing games like Ark: Survival Evolved where enemies just beeline straight for you and hit you it's actually kind of terrifying how the haybots in this game can clown-car out of a building, run up to you, and then all circle around you like a pack of wolves trying to limit your movement options. They don't just run up and attack you, they actually kite YOU and try to bait YOU into attacking them so they can retaliate.

One big warning I should give right now though is how unstable the physics can be and how limiting a lot of the tools the game has are. Parts clip through eachother far too easily which makes trying to make a train or any sort of machine with interlocking parts like a piston powered by rotational force completely unviable. They just clip straight out of their housing with a big middle finger held up. If you have something spinning fast enough (which isn't difficult) then rather than hitting enemies or flinging you it just clips straight through them. It's maddening.
Additionally, the action sequencers in the game have very limited functions such as only having a max speed of 1 second per action (which means any complex sequences are gonna take like 10 whole seconds), the timers work in an irritating and strange way, engines can only power one direction when hooked up remotely, the entire friction system is jank and unreliable with even sliding along on perfectly flat terrain bumping like crazy, and a million other pet peeves with the system. If you're a veteran of LittleBigPlanet 2 or Gmod then these limitations are going to drive you up the wall unless you want to treat them like a challenge like me.

Either way, I hope with all my heart they fix/change these issues in the future, and despite them I'm probably going to put a lot of time into this game. It's got a lot of character and it's nice to play a game that has more polish than the usual survival crafting fare you find on Steam. Even as it stands right now it's pretty fun and lacking in the sloggy bullshit that most survival crafting games have.

Pros:
- The game has 3 modes; Challenge, Survival and Creative. Its always good that i can change modes when i get bored playing the other one.
- The game offer so much freedom in building stuff. You can build bases, farms and pretty much any contraptions that you can think of, either for the reason of progressing your game in survival mode, automating and defending your farm, transporting goods or even if you just want to have fun and test out what's in your curious mind in creative mode.
- In creative mode, you can share your creations in steam workshop and of course vice versa, you can also download shared creations and spawn it into your world.
- Also in creative mode, you can customize tiles to create your own world. You can freely customize the assets, terrains, ground textures/color, and more. Some examples of the tiles I've seen and downloaded are; mario kart racetracks, runways for flying creations, mountain racetracks, rocket league arena, dirt racetracks.
- The game is open for modding and there are already many mods available to choose from in the workshop to further make your creations awesome.

Cons:
- Being in early access, there are lots of bugs and optimization issues.
- Collisions in game are not optimized and can sometimes cause minor fps drops and lag
- The game can't handle big creations and can cause huge fps drops/lags or even make the game crash.
- Survival mode does not offer much in terms of an interesting gameplay content 
- In survival mode also, gathering materials for crafting can be a hassle and grindy due to optimization issues again. For example when you're mining for metals and concretes using your creation, the fps will always drop and make some of your tire bearings to be lose and floppy, and pistons to go extend and retracts randomly. Meaning you basically lose control of your creation the moment contacts between collision happens.
- Although its fun playing in multiplayer it is sad to say that it is not yet that optimized. Again with the lag and fps drops and sometimes glitches and bugs happens while playing with others.

Conclusion: 
This game has a lot of potential as a sandbox/building/crafting and even farming simulator game, its just the matter of fixing bugs, optimization, and adding more content in survival to make the game more fun and enjoyable. And so, I'll still recommend this game even though I gave it many cons. The reason for that is because I had fun creating and building stuff and playing with others. That's it. [h1]Scrap Mechanic is a sand box/ open world builder game that allows you to be an engineer or an architect, with your own transforming buildings and vehicles that you can fly and drive.[/h1]
If you like experimenting with mechanical design, and making things go from just spare parts, then Scrap Mechanic is sure to hook you instantly. But, if you are mechanically challenged don’t worry. The Devs at Axolot Games have put together a fun assortment of “smart” parts that are pre-wired to have your designs rolling, spinning, sliding, or flying in one direction or another… or every direction at once. It also provides a user handbook in your hotbar, complete with video how-to links. The building mechanics are simple and allow you to build walls and parts to scale with ease. But, expect a learning curve and a lot of laughs as you find yourself hanging upside down from trees. 

[b]Update: I originally reviewed ScrapMechanic on April, 12th. But, it has really undergone major improvements in early access and I need to clarify the current state of the game. At this time, (& even before I bought a new rig) the lag is no longer an issue at all. The devs at Axolot Games are really on the ball. What's more, they've added many features to an already great game: musical blocks to build with included. Then, of course, the heavy addiction of the fan base to creating genius mechanical works has resulted in a large collection of workshop vehicles & creations ready-made to be downloaded straight into your own world. But, the feature I like best is the fact that I am able to save my own builds as blueprints, which can then be cloned over & over again in any of my worlds with amazing ease. If you catch this game on sale during the Holiday Season, I highly recommend you put it at the top of your list of games to buy. -11/08/16[/b]


[b]Graphics/ Music: [/b]
The art is incredibly well done. The landscape is covered with a realistic style of comic book trees, rocks, and farm equipment. Music is not only upbeat, but a radio is provided and can be attached to creations on the go. But, there is no water anywhere. This would be a feature that would be highly desired, as it would allow for design of boats. In the current early access state, the graphics run a bit slow. The lag is real… especially on low-end machines. This is a factor that needs more work, and from what the devs are saying in the forum and frequent dev blogs, it is a priority. They’ve doubled their team size this month, and while they are still adding new features constantly, they are also busy improving existing features in the program.  I’ve noticed the game runs faster on my pc already in just the couple of weeks I’ve been playing. Other early access games I’ve played started out with similar lag, but were soon running with ease for me. 

[b]Narrative:  [/b]
The survival mode story has you playing the role of a robot maintenance mechanic in space. You crash land on your first assignment on an agricultural planet where you are supposed to keep the ag-bots in working order. But, you find the place deserted and a couple of old vehicles that you can commandeer as is, or salvage for scrap parts for your own creations. This should provide more options for those players like me who have a hard time getting started with their first build. 

However, the current build has you playing in creative mode only. You can choose the terrain map, which has rolling hills and steep valleys. This seems designed much like the Disney Cars playset in Disney Infinity 1.0, (sorry, but Steam isn’t the only platform out there) very fun, lots of room to drive and do stunts, and a variety of land features. Or you can choose a flat world with nothing but dirt, for experimenting with designs or hosting mp competitions. 

[b]Combat:  [/b]
There seems to be no combat in the game at all at the moment. I haven’t found any indication of plans in this area either. The character takes no fall damage, and is not affected by hunger. Sunshine and noon are static for the time being. I assume the pending “survival mode” will include dynamic weather, and a day/night cycle, as well as other needs.  I also hope vehicular combat will be an option. 

[b]Multiplayer:  [/b]
You are able to invite friends into your game with ease. This seems to be functioning well. I also discovered that you can go into the flat sandbox, set limits on the number of parts each player is allowed to use on their vehicle, and host a design competition with friends. This provides infinite options for hours of mp fun, as well as the ability to design your own world and even race tracks.

[b]Pros:  [/b]
•	Creative, fun, and highly playable as is
•	Wide array of simple usable parts to build almost anything you can imagine
•	Flight, Mechanics, & Construction
•	Encourages trial & error
•	Suitable for all ages (even adult engineer types)
•	High replay value

[b]Cons:  [/b]
•	[i]Lag[/i] ---majorly improved, almost no lag at all now
•	No water, and limited map size in early access
•	No day/night cycle yet, creative mode only in current build
•	No combat yet

[h1]Scrap Mechanic is one of those games that I love to recommend, because it has everything to offer.[/h1] It is family friendly, creative, and fun all at the same time. It is definitely an upper tier game and worth the price, because it has tremendous replay-ability. I rate it an 8 out of 10 in the sandbox/ open world builder genre, but will probably change that rating after the final release
